DOCTORS WILL NOW GET PAID TO REPORT VACCINE INJURIES!

Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has launched a broad federal initiative focused on vaccine injuries, featuring a new research clinic at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a new medical billing code designed to reimburse doctors for reporting serious vaccine side effects. 

The program focuses on tracking and gathering data on vaccine-related adverse events through the following key components:

1. The New NIH Research Clinic
RFK Jr. established a dedicated clinic at the NIH Clinical Center in Bethesda, Maryland.

The Mission: The clinic is designed to study, evaluate, and provide care for patients who believe they have been injured by vaccines. 

Observational Studies: According to internal agency memos, the clinic will run observational studies on these patients. 

Policy Impact: RFK Jr. intends for the data gathered from this clinic to potentially inform and drive changes to the federally recommended childhood vaccine schedules. 

2. "Paying Doctors" via Medical Billing Codes
The mechanism to "pay doctors" is built around incentivizing the medical community to report suspected injuries, addressing a long-standing criticism from RFK Jr. that the current Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) is inefficient because clinicians are not compensated for the time it takes to file reports.
New Billing Code: The initiative introduces a new medical billing code through Medicare/Medicaid and private insurance systems. 

Financial Reimbursement: Doctors will be able to use this code to claim financial reimbursement for the time spent documenting and filing official reports of serious or suspected vaccine side effects. 

3. Broader Policy Context
The rollout was attended by other top administration health officials, including NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, CDC Director Erica Schwartz, and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz. This initiative coincides with separate plans by HHS to overhaul the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) and establish an explicit "injury table" for COVID-19 vaccines, allowing individuals with specified conditions to receive automatic government payouts.

Public Health Perspectives

This shows that Rahul Gandhi’s opposition is simply for the sake of opposition. When they thought the Modi government was supporting Starlink, they opposed it. Now, when they think the government is opposing it, they are supporting Starlink.

Rahul Gandhi is supporting a foreign businessman because he believes Indian businessmen are close to the Prime Minister. He seems willing to welcome a foreign businessman to challenge Indian businesses simply because he believes those businesses support Modi.

This reminds us of Jaichand. There are many such examples in Indian history where our own people sided with foreign interests to further their individual political ambitions. Every time, such choices cost the nation dearly. These divisions and betrayals contributed to centuries of foreign domination and subjugation.

Rahul Gandhi seems determined to replay the same textbook.

2108391970792161680.text:
Trump wants fewer Indian technology professionals moving to America. The unintended consequence may be more American technology work moving to India.

I have spent more than three decades in this industry. So when I read about the latest US action restricting some large technology companies from using PERM, the route through which employees move towards permanent residency, I was less worried than the headlines suggested.

One number explains why. Indian IT companies accounted for less than 1,400 of the 117,849 PERM certifications last year. Less than 2%. The direct impact may therefore be smaller than it first appears.

But something more interesting is happening underneath.

The original Indian IT model was simple. The customer had important work in America, so we sent Indian engineers there to do it. Then we discovered that much of that work could be done from India. The onsite-offshore model was born. I lived that transition.

We may be at the beginning of another one.

America is making it harder to move Indian talent there, while technology is making it easier for smaller teams in India to take responsibility for increasingly sophisticated work.

There is an irony here. In trying to reduce the movement of Indian talent to America, the US may accelerate the movement of American work to India.

But I don’t mean another wave of coding and maintenance jobs.

The opportunity is architecture, product engineering, cybersecurity, AI implementation, industry solutions and eventually ownership of products and IP.

Indian teams should not merely receive specifications from New York. They should help decide what gets built. Not merely maintain a global bank’s technology platform, but help redesign the bank. Not just supply engineers to solve somebody else’s problem, but own the problem.

There is an uncomfortable truth too.

For thirty years, growth in Indian IT and growth in Indian IT employment travelled together. Win more business, hire more engineers.

As AI technology improves productivity, that relationship may weaken. Indian IT could win more sophisticated work and create more value without headcount growing at the same rate.

So we need a different definition of success.

For thirty years, Indian IT competed largely on the cost of Indian talent. The next thirty will depend on the capability of Indian talent.

Can we create architects rather than only programmers? Build products and IP here? Move more global decision-making to India? Create more value per person and therefore pay our people far better?

Those are much bigger questions than how many visas America issues.

So worry not about the visa headlines.

Trump may make it harder for Indian engineers to move to American work. The opportunity is to make American work move to Indian engineers.

In 1993, this photo of Belgian soldiers holding a Somali boy over an open fire shocked the world.

The soldiers were in Mogadishu as part of the UN-authorized Operation Restore Hope, supposedly there to protect Somalis and deliver humanitarian assistance.

The photograph became evidence in a military prosecution.

And what happened next was even more shocking.

In June 1997, a Belgian military court acquitted the two soldiers, Claude Baert and Kurt Coelus, of assault, battery and threats.

Their defence?

They claimed it was merely a “game.”

The court accepted that there was insufficient evidence that the boy had suffered bodily harm or that his life had been threatened.

The prosecution appealed.

In December 1997, the acquittal was confirmed.

Imagine being the Somali child in that photograph.

Imagine watching the men who held you over a fire walk free because a court decided there was insufficient proof that you had been harmed.

This is part of the history that disappears when Western military interventions in Africa are remembered only through the language of “peacekeeping” and “humanitarianism.”

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. 2108056795608748076.text:
The best pitcher in baseball refuses to lift weights, warms up by throwing a javelin, and scouts hitters with a paper notebook. The Dodgers paid him $325 million and then hired his sensei too.

The notebook makes sense once you see the rest of his system.

Yamamoto trains under Osamu Yada, who has never told him to touch a barbell. Javelin throws instead of long toss. Handstands, back bridges, breathing work. The Dodgers studied the routine, decided they couldn't improve it, and hired Yada rather than change Yamamoto. During free agency, one team's recruiting gift to him was a team-logoed javelin, just to prove how deep their research went.

The results broke baseball's assumptions. Last November he threw 96 pitches in World Series Game 6, then came out of the bullpen and closed Game 7 the very next day.

Now look at the dugout. Every MLB club runs Hawk-Eye, a dozen cameras per stadium tracking spin, tilt, and swing path on every single pitch. Yamamoto has all of it on an iPad ten feet away.

He writes by hand anyway.

Japanese player development bakes this in. Kids keep baseball journals from little league on, charting every at-bat in their own words. The logic survives contact with analytics. League data tells you what a hitter does on average. A pitcher's own notes capture what that hitter did against him tonight, pitch by pitch, while the at-bat is still fresh. By the third time through the order, he's working from a document no analytics department can generate.

Mookie Betts watched this for two seasons. This spring he started throwing javelins too.

Baseball built the most surveilled playing field in sports. Its best October pitcher still trusts the notebook in his back pocket more.

A note from our research leaders:

Last week we parted ways with Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek after a thorough investigation found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information. Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what’s outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment. We generally keep individual employment matters private and don't believe a back and forth would be productive or lead to a resolution, but we want to address the points they raised in their letter directly.

- We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical. We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions. We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust. We will continue to be extremely forgiving of our team making good-faith mistakes. We have not and do not terminate any of our employees for raising concerns.

- We are actively finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors and will announce details in the coming weeks. People across the company have been working really hard on getting these partnerships up and running. We are committed to embedding external assessors and continue to make close collaboration with independent safety organizations a core part of our safety work. Many of our researchers already work with 3p safety organizations productively.

- We agree with the letter that preserving the monitorability of frontier models requires an industry-wide commitment, including from OpenAI. Monitorability has long been a core piece of our research program, and something we continue to invest significant resources in (see our publications on Monitoring Monitorability and the subsequent open sourcing of monitorability evals, our system card for GPT-6 Astra, Jakub’s blog and post on X, and the numerous blog posts on our Alignment blog on the topic).

We are deeply sad about this outcome. We appreciated Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek’s contributions to AI safety at OpenAI and their willingness to speak up and challenge ideas. We championed their voices, supported their work, and placed enormous trust in them. These decisions were not about them raising safety concerns. We have always encouraged that and always will.

If you’re surprised Caitlin Clark got snubbed in the WNBA MVP voting on Thursday, then you haven’t been paying attention to the league. Clark put up offensive numbers nobody in the league has ever managed, and yet 19 of the 74 voters decided she wasn’t one of the five best players in the league.

A’ja Wilson charged a fan in the stands, got a technical, and got the MVP. That’s the WNBA. Rudeness gets the trophy. The class act gets left off the ballot.

Wilson won her fifth MVP and took 65 of 74 first-place votes. She led the league at 26.2 points and 1.9 blocks as a center. Her numbers are real. So is her bad behavior.

Wilson got a pass for charging a fan during a game and screaming at him. That in itself tells you all you need to know about the WNBA. On September 29, Game 2 in Indianapolis, a fan pointed and said the foul was on her. Wilson left the play, crossed the baseline, pointed back, and shouted at him. Teammates and security pulled her off it. She got a technical. The fan was walked out, then let back in. No suspension for Wilson.

Clark averaged 22.3 points and 8.3 assists. She’s the first player in league history to finish a season at 20 and 8. She got one first-place vote. She finished fourth, behind Wilson, Olivia Miles, and her own teammate Kelsey Mitchell.

Nineteen of the 74 voters left her off the ballot entirely. She showed up on 55. One first, six seconds, 20 thirds, 16 fourths, 12 fifths, 212 points. Miles had 442. Mitchell had 287.

A voter can put Wilson first based on numbers, but not on behavior. A voter can’t watch Clark achieve the first 20-and-8 season the league has ever had and still leave her off a five-player ballot, like those 19 voters did. That’s not a ranking. That’s leaving Clark out on purpose. Sophie Cunningham said Saturday that something should’ve happened to Wilson when she charged a fan, and that Wilson is the LeBron of the league, so it didn’t. Cunningham was right.

This is why the WNBA doesn’t get respect. It glorifies the player who charges a customer and shrugs at the one who set a record. Wilson got the trophy nine days after the technical. Clark got erased by 19 people with a ballot. The WNBA props up its disgraceful players and ignores its true professionals. That’s why you should ignore the WNBA.

In general, I have never seen Prime Minister Modi give negative signals in public.

I felt the seriousness when he said this in May:

"First came the corona pandemic; then wars began to break out, and now there is an energy crisis. This decade is turning into a decade of disasters for the world.

If these situations are not rapidly changed, the achievements of the past many decades would be washed away, and a huge section of the world’s population would be pushed back into poverty."

It is five months since he said this. Things have only become much worse in that period.

The relationship with the United States is at all time low, and one can even argue that America is now hostile to India.

America wanted a relationship with India to balance China’s power.

China is now in a different league. The revived term for the United States and China is “G2.” So the argument runs that the US no longer sees any "use" for India.

The US has been a major export market and a provider of capital and technology for India.

So I believe the US will only try to create more problems and difficulties for our country.

India has been aware of this shift, though it has only recently begun to give formal, fitting responses to America.

India has developed several sources for its energy and fertiliser needs.

We are also trying to create and expand new markets for our exports.

But with El Nino, high inflation, interest rate hikes, huge shipping costs, supply chains breaking down and pushing up prices for many things, including food, rupee depreciation, and capital outflows, we face many headwinds.

Added to this is AI disruption of white collar jobs.

As I shared recently, everyone from a PMO official to the Chief Economic Adviser to the External Affairs Minister has conveyed the above, in different words and as mildly as possible.

There is not much an individual can do.

As I have been repeating, an emergency fund to cover three years of expenses, not borrowing, spending on needs, and postponing wants until better times are what we can do.

As a country, we need to face this tough period together.

If you read economic history and cycles, you realise these kinds of tough times do not last forever.

In good times, we think they will continue forever.

In bad times, we think we are doomed forever.

Neither is true.

Everything is a cycle.

No one can avoid cycles.

The best we can do, as individuals, companies, or a country, is to be as prepared as our circumstances allow to face those cycles.

Banyak yang ngira ini murni drama fans ngambek gara-gara T.O.P go public pacaran sama Nana. 

Ternyata aslinya jauh lebih toxic dari itu.

Menurut CHOIDOT, isu kencan cuma jadi pemicu meledaknya bom waktu dari kebobrokan agensi T.O.P (TOPSPOT PICTURES) yang selama ini ngejadiin fansite sebagai 'babu gratisan'.

Berikut 'dosa-dosa' agensinya dan kenapa fansite ini akhirnya fed up 👇

1. Agensi Lepas Tangan & Fansite Dijadiin CS Gratisan.

TOPSPOT PICTURES sama sekali nggak punya saluran komunikasi resmi kayak email atau komunitas fans. Ujung-ujungnya, fansite yang harus turun tangan jadi penghubung, bahkan sampai ngurusin pertanyaan dari fans global.

2. Eksploitasi Duit & Waktu Fansite.

Fansite patungan ngumpulin dana sampai 10 juta won buat pasang iklan comeback T.O.P di 8 titik lokasi yang berbeda. Lucunya, agensi malah nggak ketahuan pasang iklan di mana, tapi berani-beraninya ikut campur ngerevisi desain iklan bikinan fansite sampai larut malam.

3. Fansite Disuruh Jadi 'Polisi' & Event Organizer.

Agensi sering banget nyuruh fansite buat nertibin fans lain, kayak minta tolong hapusin foto-foto unofficial di medsos. Nggak cuma itu, saking nggak punya staf profesional yang mumpuni, agensi sampai minta saran teknis ke fansite buat ngurus acara, termasuk nanya link beli gelas sampanye.

4. Minta Materi Tapi Dighosting

Pas ada event resmi, agensi minta foto resolusi tinggi ke fansite buat diposting di Fanclub Jepang. Fansite udah gercep ngirimin, eh ujung-ujungnya foto itu nggak pernah diposting atau dipakai sama sekali.

5. Nutupin Promosi & Konser yang Bobrok.

Tiket VIP di Hong Kong dijual mahal banget (sekitar 300 ribu won), tapi benefitnya ampas (cuma soundcheck 5 menit & send-off 30 detik). Pas fans ngamuk minta refund, agensi nggak nyediain tempat komplain, jadi fansite lagi-lagi yang jadi tameng sasaran marah. Terus pas konser di Taipei sepi penonton, agensi ketahuan upload foto editan manipulasi cahaya buat nutupin kursi kosong, yang akhirnya buru-buru dihapus.

6. Puncak Masalah (Tragedi Batal Pameran)

Fansite bikin pameran pakai uang pribadi dengan modal awal sekitar 9 juta won. Dari awal peminatnya emang lesu, cuma 20an orang yang daftar di minggu pertama. Nah, pas berita kencan T.O.P & Nana rilis, badai cancelation makin parah sampai sisa 10-15% peserta per hari. Fansite nombok rugi sampai 7 juta Won dan akhirnya terpaksa ngebatalin acara.

7. Agensi Gaslighting & Playing Victim

Fansite sebenernya udah tahu T.O.P pacaran dari lama dan diam aja demi ngehargain privasi artis. Demi transparansi dan biar fans luar negeri nggak rugi tiket pesawat, fansite ngumumin alasan batalnya pameran karena sepi peminat. Bukannya instrospeksi, agensinya malah ngamuk karena masalah reservation rate yang rendah itu dibongkar ke publik. Agensi lalu mendistorsi fakta seolah-olah fansite tutup murni karena fans marah idolnya pacaran.

8. Kekecewaan Mendalam Sama T.O.P

Fansite ngerasa T.O.P nggak nepatin janji. Katanya bikin album buat fans, tapi 5 bulan rilis malah nggak ada panggung atau komunikasi sama sekali. Fansite merasa T.O.P cuma mau dengerin orang-orang yang 'asal bapak senang' dan nganggep dukungan fans itu hal yang otomatis ada kapanpun dia butuh.

Hmmmmm~ pelik juga ya masalahnya 🤔

Most of the recent math results were not reached by a swarm, the way Navier–Stokes was. I think that part got lost in the excitement around the release. OpenAI's unnamed internal model, which I'm going to call Aeon, reached most of them in one shot, from a single prompt, with no interruptions. This model did not even exist before the end of August, and it is still training. Notice how the returns are not dropping off? That chart is from a month ago. It is a log scale. What does Aeon look like now? 

On average, each result used three hours of thinking. Aeon was given 4000 problems to work on by OpenAI. How many more have been solved in the last three days? That number is not zero. 

It's like hearing notes in a song that is slowly rising. I don't think Pacing the Frontier was just about Hugging Face or hacking. They've seen how close we are to closing the loop, and as the hour draws near, their resolve begins to quaver. The last piece was model creativity, and I think that threshold was crossed internally by Anthropic and OpenAI in September. You see it in Opus 5.5, which gets it from Fable 5.5. You see it in the math results from Aeon.

All that was needed to start the event was the ability for models to think of novel ways to improve themselves. That was the last piece. This is directly analogous to the ability to think of strange, alien ways to solve math problems: solutions so inhuman that they are difficult to express in existing human terms, so the proof winds up incomprehensible. I think these same kinds of alien solutions are now being applied to model improvements internally. That's what all this recent consternation is really about. They see the invisible frontier. And they see what is about to happen.

This dude does a traffic stop on a deputy. You can see the moment in the officers face when he realizes he is in violation of the law.

​ A Grant County sheriff’s deputy is flagged down after being spotted patrolling in an unmarked Dodge Charger. What starts as a standard roadside encounter quickly pivots into an educational clinic on state law.

Gavin ​Seim presses the deputy on Revised Code of Washington (RCW) 46.08.065, which strictly governs public vehicle markings and limits unmarked cars to undercover or confidential investigative duties. When the deputy admits he routinely uses the car for ordinary traffic stops, the scenario shifts completely. You can see the exact moment the realization sets in across the officer’s face—the subtle shift from polite skepticism to genuine bewilderment as the statutory language sinks in.

​Instead of escalating or flexing authority, the deputy actually listens, checks the credentials, and takes in the reality that the man on the roadside has the law dead-to-rights. By the end, Seim lets the deputy off with a verbal "warning" and advises him to park the cruiser back at the station.

​It’s wild how unaware of the law so many of our officers are, but yet they are trusted with enforcement and upholding laws they have little to no knowledge of.

I’ve seen enough people ask that I’ll break down the math. 

Brandon Aubrey XP%: 97%
NFL average 2Pt rate: 48%

Key assumptions: You score twice and get stops. OT win probability is 50%

If you kick the XP twice, you have a 95% chance of sending game to OT, 50% chance of winning in OT. 47.5% chance at winning the game.

If you go for two:

Get first, kick XP on second and win in regulation: 46.6% of time, win 100%

Get first, miss XP and go to OT: 1.4% of time, win 50%

Miss first, get second and go to OT: 24.9% of time, win 50% of time

Miss first and second 2-Point: 27.6% of time, guaranteed loss

By going for two, your win probability jumps to 59.8% chance.

So if you guarantee me we get two scores and two stops, you’ll win ~47% of the time kicking extra points, and ~60% of the time going for two.

The reason it doesn’t jive with coaches/fans is because delaying a loss feels psychologically advantageous… but losing in OT vs losing in regulation is the same result

1868716440691360135.text:
(I'll use this post in the future for future reference as people *keep* asking me on my thoughts on this topic. These are my thoughts -- again -- on Xbox' multiplatform strategy.)

It's funny they call it Project Latitude, because that suggests they primarily only see the growth width their strategy might give them. Modern Microsoft is almost completely driven by data and research, not so much by the ability to recognize intangible effects or broader social developments, something many of us would call common sense. Over 20 years of Xbox legacy have proven that again and again, unfortunately.

Releasing a game on multiple platforms, making it available to more potential players, will result in more up-front revenue in any kind of possible calculation. That's just maths. The side effects beyond those numbers are a completely different story though.

The new multiplatform approach by Xbox comes with its own costs, from added development challenges (hello Sea of Thieves in 2024) to the most important one: the potential loss of your own identity and with that the loss of customers to other ecosystems.

There is a very strong belief within Xbox that players locked into an ecosystem won't change their platform because of their existing library etc (which 20+ Million Xbox players barely build anymore these days because of Game Pass). Not only do I believe is this nonsense especially mid- to long-term -- as new games will always matter more the longer time goes on -- more importantly, it also completely ignores new players joining gaming every day. The gaming community today is not the same community it is in 5, 10 or 15 years from today. Players decide which ecosystem to invest their money in every day. And if there is one ecosystem where I can play Marvel's Blade and one ecosystem where I can play both Marvel's Blade and Marvel's Wolverine, people sure as hell would know where to put their money in.

Halo, Gears of War, Forza Motorsport/Horizon, Sea of Thieves, Fable etc... These IP became multi-million IPs on Xbox. And only on Xbox. The same goes for dozens of successful IPs on Playstation and Nintendo systems.

I said it again and again: in an ideal world, there wouldn't be exclusive games and everyone can play everything, everywhere, on every device. But that's not the reality, and with Sony and Nintendo, it won't be any time soon. This is a one-way street, and Xbox might simply be way too early... again.

I do feel like Xbox can not do roundtables or business updates and say things like "our fans should know this is all about delivering exclusive games to platforms where Game Pass exists" or "this is not a core change to our strategy to exclusives" when... A few months later, none of that is true. That feels like a punch in the face to those who carried this platform for over 20 years. People are starting to call this is them lying, and honestly, while I wouldn't go that far... I get it.

I'm highly energized by the games Xbox has cooking. Their line-up is incredibly strong, I do believe they are on the right path here. I'll keep sharing my excitement for these teams and their games, because at its core, I'll be able to play all of these and great games is everything this should be about.

Following the acquisition of ABK, Xbox has growth pressure. I think we all get that. The way to get there is highly debatable though. Exclusives matter, period. You don't see Netflix, Disney+ or whatever working without exclusives either. I question their strategy or at least their selection of games and the corresponding announcement strategy. Gaming is a pillar at Microsoft and that won't change. The only question is whether that future is called Xbox or... Microsoft Gaming.

Here's a curious thing that happens when you try mixing liquids that won't chemically blend, like water and oil 🧪 On Earth, oil floats on top of water because of the difference in density. In space, there's no weight from gravity, so that natural separation never happens. The two liquids stay mixed together as a floating suspension of droplets, until rotation steps in: spin the container, and inertia pushes the denser water outward while the oil gathers toward the center 🌀🌌

Microgravity turns everyday physics upside down ✨🚀

2108671949324816741.text:
Bill Gates offered his childhood friend Paul Allen $5 per share to buy him out of Microsoft. Allen refused and kept the stock that would eventually help make him worth an estimated $40B.

Months earlier, while Allen was undergoing cancer treatment, he had overheard Gates and Steve Ballmer discussing how to reduce his ownership in the company they had built together.

The 2 had known each other since school.

Allen was 15 when he met 13-year-old Gates. They spent their teenage years working with computers and eventually founded Microsoft in 1975.

But the ownership split had been a source of tension from the beginning.

Gates initially wanted 60% of the company.

Allen got 40%.

Later, Gates pushed for another adjustment.

64% for himself.

36% for Allen.

Allen agreed.

Microsoft kept growing. Its deal to supply software for IBM's personal computer put the business on a completely different trajectory.

Then, in 1982, Allen was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma.

He began radiation treatment and gradually reduced his involvement in the company.

One evening in December, he walked past Gates' office.

Gates was talking with Steve Ballmer.

According to Allen, they were discussing his reduced productivity and how they could dilute his Microsoft equity by issuing stock options to themselves and others.

Allen stopped outside the door and listened.

Then he walked in.

He confronted both men and left.

That evening, Ballmer came to his house to apologize.

Days later, Gates sent a handwritten apology.

6 pages long.

But Allen had decided to leave.

In February 1983, he resigned from Microsoft.

Gates offered to buy his shares for $5 each.

Allen wanted at least $10.

Gates wouldn't pay it.

So Allen kept his stock.

When Microsoft went public in 1986, Allen still owned roughly 25% of the company.

As Microsoft grew into one of the world's largest businesses, his shares made him one of the richest people alive.

At one point, his fortune was estimated at $40B.

The 2 friends eventually repaired their relationship.

But Allen never forgot the conversation he overheard during his cancer treatment.

Gates had offered him $5 a share to leave.

Allen left.

His shares stayed.

SNL TURNED A WHITE HOUSE RENOVATION INTO A HOME-IMPROVEMENT SHOW.

And that format choice is what makes the premise interesting.

“White House Makeover” takes the familiar language of property-renovation television and applies it to Trump's plans for the White House ballroom.

Instead of treating the subject like a conventional political report, the sketch borrows a format audiences recognize immediately.

The makeover reveal.

The confident hosts.

The promise that a big renovation will solve everything.

But the White House isn't an ordinary house, and a presidential building project isn't just another television renovation.

That contrast gives the satire its starting point.

SNL takes a political story and changes the lens through which we see it.

Suddenly, a question about presidential priorities becomes a parody of television's obsession with dramatic transformations.

Mine de rien, je pense qu'Elon Musk est en train de poser les bases d'une philosophie extrêmement solide. Et très peu de gens l'ont remarqué.

Petit retour en arrière.

Le christianisme nous a laissé un socle de valeurs qui a rendu possible tout le reste. Il y avait la dignité de l'individu et la valeur du travail. Il y avait aussi l'idée que le monde est ordonné, donc intelligible. Les premiers scientifiques cherchaient à lire les lois d'un créateur. Sans ce socle, il n'y aurait pas eu de méthode scientifique ni de révolution industrielle.

Puis Nietzsche arrive : Dieu est mort. Et il ne le dit pas en triomphant. Il prévient : on vient de scier la branche sur laquelle on était assis, et rien ne la remplace. Ce qui vient après, c'est le nihilisme.

150 ans plus tard, on y est. Le débat public est coincé entre deux camps qui ne se parlent plus. D'un côté, des religieux qui défendent des dogmes que beaucoup ne peuvent plus croire au pied de la lettre. De l'autre, un matérialisme intégriste qui croit avoir déjà tout compris. Pour lui, l'univers est une machine et la conscience une illusion, donc il n'y a rien de plus à chercher.

Ce deuxième intégrisme est à mon avis le plus dangereux, parce qu'il se fait passer pour de la science. Or la vraie science ne ferme jamais une question. Et la conscience est probablement la plus grande question ouverte qui existe. Personne ne sait ce que c'est. Prétendre le contraire, ce n'est pas du scepticisme, c'est un dogme.

C'est là que l'approche d'Elon devient intéressante. La mission de xAI, c'est de comprendre la vraie nature de l'univers. Ça ressemble à un slogan, mais c'est en réalité une philosophie complète.

Elle dit trois choses. Il existe une vérité. Elle vaut la peine d'être cherchée. Et la chercher est la chose la plus noble qu'une civilisation puisse faire.

Ça rejoint directement la phrase la plus puissante du christianisme : « La vérité vous rendra libre. » C'est la même boussole morale, mais sans obligation d'adhérer à un dogme. En même temps, le scepticisme scientifique reste le moteur. On ne présuppose pas la réponse, on la découvre.

Ce n'est ni l'Église, ni le matérialisme. C'est une troisième voie. Et elle convient parfaitement à quelqu'un d'agnostique, qui dit simplement : je ne sais pas encore, mais je veux savoir.

Maintenant, ajoutez la superintelligence.

Pour la première fois, on va avoir un outil capable de s'attaquer aux questions qu'on a mises de côté depuis des siècles, faute de moyens. Quelle est la nature de l'espace et du temps ? Qu'y a-t-il sous la physique qu'on connaît ? Qu'est-ce que la conscience humaine, réellement ? Chacune de ces réponses sera un bond en avant comparable à Newton ou Einstein. Peut-être plus grand encore.

C'est exactement la philosophie dont a besoin une civilisation qui veut monter sur l'échelle de Kardashev. Une civilisation de type 2 maîtrise l'énergie de son étoile, une civilisation de type 3 celle de sa galaxie. On n'y arrive pas avec du nihilisme, ni avec des dogmes figés. On y arrive avec une curiosité sans limite et de l'humilité face à ce qu'on ne sait pas. Il faut aussi la conviction que la vérité vaut tous les efforts.

Nietzsche avait posé la question : par quoi remplacer Dieu comme source de sens ?

La réponse est peut-être sous nos yeux. Ce n'est pas une nouvelle religion, c'est une quête : comprendre l'univers.

Yesterday, an ICE agent opened fire in Marble Hill. They shot a member of our community in the neck while he was in his car. His five-year-old kid was in a child seat in the back of the car when ICE agents fired at least 7 rounds into it. This was in the middle of the afternoon, with children walking home from school and people heading home from work. Federal agents put every one of them in danger.

When I was in Marble Hill last night I saw NYPD officers rapidly escalating violence. As I was trying to de-escalate, I was shoved to the ground by an officer. I witnessed unmarked law enforcement cars hitting protestors as NYPD officers pushed people out of its path. And instead of condemning ICE’s violence, Police Commissioner Tisch attempted to justify the shooting by reading off our neighbor’s past interactions with police.

The NYPD spent more time protecting a militia that just shot someone than protecting New Yorkers. Last night, the NYPD and Commissioner Tisch violated the spirit, if not the letter, of our sanctuary city policies and fueled the Trump Administration’s attempt to demonize our communities. The NYPD’s Strategic Response Group must be disbanded as quickly as possible, and Commissioner Tisch must step down.

In this district, there are mothers who are afraid to send their kids to school, workers who are afraid to show up for their shifts, and people who won’t call for help anymore because they can’t be sure who will come. That’s what it means to have a violent militia operating in your community. You don’t feel safe walking down your own street. 

For decades, we’ve been told ICE can be fixed with more oversight, better training, or reform. But you can’t reform an agency whose purpose is to terrorize immigrant families. You can’t train cruelty out of a system built to enact cruelty. ICE must be abolished.

This moment demands that everyone step up. Elected officials at every level need to stop hedging and say it plainly: Abolish ICE now. Our city must enforce every sanctuary protection we have and city officials must ensure this cannot happen again.

Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers.

Eight hours is how long the evacuation reportedly took. Tim Kennedy, a Green Beret and former UFC fighter, was hit three times in the leg on September 17, in an ambush in South Kivu that killed at least seven Congolese and a New Zealand SAS veteran, Justin Conaglen, who had left the military only weeks earlier. A third operator was wounded. Kennedy is now at Walter Reed in stable condition, and New Zealand has opened its own investigation into Conaglen's death.

The mission is worth reading twice. Eastern Congo holds cobalt, copper and gold, the raw material of every phone and electric car battery, and the region has been at war over it for decades. M23, which the UN says Rwanda backs, took Goma and Bukavu last year. Congo's answer was to hire help. Vectus Global, a firm linked to Blackwater founder Erik Prince, was brought in to protect mining revenue, and its work has since drifted toward military operations. Reuters reports this was its first casualty event in the country.

Who fired is the part still unsettled. Three Reuters sources say the ambush was too sophisticated for anyone but Rwandan forces, and one says the attackers may have followed a surveillance drone to the team's location. A competing rumor names Russia's Africa Corps, the successor to Wagner. No one has produced proof of that, and the reporting points the other way.

The detail I keep returning to is smaller. As of last year, Kennedy was a part-time master sergeant in the Maryland National Guard. If that has not changed, a serving American soldier was shot while working private security for a foreign government. Guard members can hold civilian jobs, so the question is not whether that is allowed in principle. It is whether anyone in uniform knew, and whether anyone approved it.

Someone signed off, or no one did. Either answer is the story.

All of it is reportedly sourced to anonymous officials, and Kennedy, Vectus and the Pentagon have not commented.

Some further thoughts on the new round of peace negotiations with Putin over Ukraine.

Moscow is offering the United States not "peace in exchange for business," but rather "business in exchange for war." The Kremlin is offering Washington major Russian-American deals, access to energy resources, the Arctic, critical minerals, infrastructure and investment projects. The main objective is to buy American consent to the normalization of the war Russia is waging against Ukraine.

Kirill Dmitriev is effectively selling Washington precisely this model of future relations. The head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund and Putin’s special envoy has been systematically working through the channels of Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, whose value lies exactly in their direct access to Trump’s inner circle. Following the meeting with Putin on September 5, the Kremlin once again separately reported that major Russian-American projects had been discussed in detail.

At the same time, Moscow is offering an entire package of economic "normalization." It includes Arctic oil and gas, LNG, heavy oil, lithium, copper, nickel, platinum, rare earth metals, nuclear energy, infrastructure and aviation. Long-term purchases of American aircraft have been discussed, which would require the lifting of aviation sanctions, as well as compensation for American companies for losses incurred after leaving Russia.

Energy and the Arctic are the central components of the proposal because this is where Russian and American interests could potentially be linked for decades. Russia needs technology, capital and sanctions relief to develop difficult oil and gas fields and LNG projects. American companies are being offered access to resources. For the Kremlin, the main benefit would come when American companies invest billions of their own dollars in these projects. After that, imposing new sanctions on Russia would also mean losses for American businesses.

Sakhalin-1 demonstrates how Moscow is trying to create such mutual interests in practice. On August 15, 2025, the day of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage, Putin signed Decree No. 559, which opened a legal pathway for the return of foreign investors. For Exxon, this concerns its former 30% stake and approximately $4.6 billion written off after the company left Russia. Exxon has publicly denied plans to return, but talks continued: Reuters reported on a non-binding framework agreement between Exxon and Rosneft, while the Wall Street Journal reported contacts between Neil Chapman and Igor Sechin, and Darren Woods discussed the issue with Trump. Putin has meanwhile extended the deadline for transactions involving the stake until January 1, 2027. Moscow is effectively offering Exxon the opportunity to recover billions in lost value in exchange for restoring an economic relationship with Russia.

Gentry Beach and Novatek show that such a model can be put into practice. According to The New York Times, the Dallas-based investor, who has ties to the Trump family, signed an LNG agreement with Novatek after the Anchorage summit. Beach himself said that the project had been discussed “at the highest levels” in Moscow and Washington. This is already a concrete American private-sector interest for which improved relations with Russia have financial value.

Moscow is using critical minerals to exploit American dependence on China. Putin has offered American companies access to Russian deposits of lithium, nickel, platinum and rare earth metals. But in February 2025, he explicitly included the so-called “new territories” - the Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia - in the proposal. This makes the Russian offer particularly revealing: American businesses are effectively being offered an economic interest in resources located in territories seized by Russia as a result of the war.

The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant illustrates even more clearly how business can become an instrument for normalizing the consequences of the war. Bloomberg reported on options involving American participation in or control over the plant, with the electricity it generates potentially being divided between the parties. In other words, a Ukrainian facility seized by Russia is no longer being discussed solely as an issue of occupation, but also as the subject of a potential economic agreement.

Even the proposals concerning aluminum follow the same model - access to the Russian market in exchange for the lifting of restrictions. In February 2025, Putin proposed returning approximately 2 million tonnes of Russian aluminum per year to the US market.

Separately, he proposed an approximately $15 billion project in Russia’s Krasnoyarsk Krai involving a hydroelectric power plant and new aluminum production.

There are also more extravagant proposals designed to sell Trump the image of a grand historic deal. In October 2025, Dmitriev proposed a “Putin-Trump tunnel” beneath the Bering Strait: 112 km long, costing approximately $8 billion and taking up to eight years to build, potentially with the involvement of Elon Musk’s Boring Company. The economic feasibility of such an estimate is questionable. But the political product is obvious: a major project, Trump’s name and a symbol of a new US-Russia partnership.

The same function is served by the $14 trillion figure Dmitriev uses to describe the potential of economic cooperation. It emerged after Zelenskyy said on February 6, 2026, that Ukrainian intelligence had obtained documents concerning a so-called “Dmitriev package” worth approximately $12 trillion. Following The Economist’s publication, Dmitriev called the $12 trillion figure “fake news,” but immediately raised the estimate to more than $14 trillion and claimed that American businesses had already lost more than $300 billion because of sanctions. There is no documentary evidence confirming the realism of this figure. For now, it is a populist argument aimed at an American audience: confrontation with Russia costs you money, while cooperation could bring in far more.

And American capital is already responding to the opportunities, although so far largely outside Russia itself. On January 29, 2026, Lukoil announced a deal with Carlyle to sell LUKOIL International GmbH, which holds international assets with a book value of approximately $22 billion. The deal is subject to OFAC approval. Reuters also reported competing bids from Chevron and Quantum Capital, as well as interest from Exxon and ADNOC. In other words, when Russian assets become available and the Treasury allows a transaction to proceed, major American businesses immediately show interest.

On the other hand, the Carlyle example currently demonstrates the willingness of American capital to buy Russian assets, rather than the willingness to invest in Russia. Lukoil is selling its foreign assets precisely because of sanctions pressure. This is effectively a consequence of pressure on Russia, rather than evidence of successful normalization. For the Kremlin, the next step is much more important: to ensure that American money flows not into the purchase of assets from Russia, but into new projects inside Russia itself.

OFAC demonstrated another vulnerability in the sanctions system in 2026: American interests can outweigh the desire to maintain pressure on Russia. In March, General Licenses 133 and 134 were issued, followed later by 134B and 134C, allowing transactions involving certain shipments of Russian oil, including cargoes belonging to Rosneft, Lukoil and sanctioned tankers. The reason was the US-Israeli war against Iran, problems surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and the threat of an oil shortage. Dmitriev did not cause this. But Moscow saw the lesson clearly: if Russian oil is needed by the US to solve another problem, sanctions can become secondary.

The main obstacle to the Russian model currently lies in Congress. On August 7, the Senate voted 86-11 in favor of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which provides for increased pressure on Russia’s energy sector, financial system, shadow fleet and major buyers of Russian energy. A companion bill introduced by McCaul and Hoyer has already been submitted to the House of Representatives. The 86-11 vote shows that, outside the president’s inner circle, the idea of a rapid return to business as usual with Russia does not yet have political consensus.

Moscow is therefore not currently working with the entire American system, but with its most receptive elements.

Opposing this are a significant part of Congress and the security establishment. The Treasury Department is taking a more situational approach: sanctions can be eased when broader American interests require it.

Why does Moscow need economic cooperation with the US if China and Chinese capital are available next door? China already buys Russian resources, but it cannot lift American sanctions, return Russia to the dollar-based financial system, or weaken the transatlantic sanctions regime. American investment offers the Kremlin much more: capital and technology, political legitimacy, less dependence on China, and potentially an American lobbying constituency interested in maintaining stable relations with Russia.

Moscow already has some initial results, but they remain contradictory.

There is Beach-Novatek, the negotiations surrounding Sakhalin-1, Carlyle and Lukoil’s international assets, interest from Chevron and Quantum, and a series of OFAC exemptions. But Carlyle is benefiting from a sanctions-driven asset sale, Exxon is seeking to recover its own losses, and OFAC eased restrictions because of an energy crisis. This is still not the systemic normalization that the Kremlin wants.

Moscow’s real success will begin when American businesses start investing new money directly into Russia and become interested in protecting those investments from future sanctions. An even more significant threshold will be reached if American capital becomes willing to enter projects connected to occupied Ukrainian territories and assets seized during the war.

The struggle is therefore no longer about whether individual US-Russia deals are possible - they are. The question is whether the Kremlin can turn these deals into a system in which American domestic interests emerge that would favor accepting Russia’s aggressive policy on the European continent.

Bloomberg has released a massive article, detailing in-depth the development of GTA 6 and why it took so long, with exclusive information that we've never heard before.

Here are the highlights:

- GTA VI has been in full development for over 8 years, making it Rockstar's biggest and most ambitious project.

- The original vision included large areas of North and South America, but the scope was eventually reduced to Vice City (Miami) and its surrounding regions.

- Rockstar initially planned to develop GTA VI alongside Red Dead Redemption 2, but RDR2 required most of the company's resources, delaying GTA VI's development.

- Rockstar shifted from developing multiple games simultaneously to focusing most of its workforce on one major game.

- Rockstar's workforce nearly doubled, growing from 2,441 employees in 2018 to 4,711 in 2026, spread across 12 offices.

- Rockstar's three heads of development are Rob Nelson, Aaron Garbut, and Phil Hooker, rather than one traditional game director.

- The game's basic story, featuring Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, was established by late 2019.

- The developers experienced a difficult early development phase, described internally as a "dark period," when the game's overall vision remained unclear.

- By 2022, enough of the game's systems had come together for the developers to begin seeing the complete vision.

- GTA VI features Rockstar's most realistic and detailed open world yet, building heavily on systems introduced in Red Dead Redemption 2

- Rockstar invested heavily in making NPCs feel believable, rather than simply populating the world with generic characters.

- The developers struggled to balance realism and entertainment, debating how interactive everyday activities should be, such as purchasing drinks or preparing food.

- Jason and Lucia can spend time together throughout the open world, rather than interacting only during scripted missions.

- Players controlling Jason can text Lucia and arrange to meet up.

- Making the couple behave naturally required complex traditional AI systems, which took years to develop.

- Rockstar considers the dynamic interactions between Jason and Lucia one of GTA VI's biggest innovations.

- GTA VI aims to balance GTA 5's chaotic, satirical gameplay with RDR2's realism and emotional storytelling.

- GTA VI's NPC systems are designed to generate unpredictable interactions and situations naturally.

- Bloomberg was shown a gameplay session by development head Phil Hooker, which emphasized this series of entirely unscripted event: He accidentally collided with another driver, Hooker attempted to visit a convenience store to recover health then another NPC insulted him, triggering a violent confrontation. he found the cash register unattended and robbed the store. Police pursued him, forcing him to abandon his vehicle so he stole another valuable vehicle intending to sell it then another vehicle blasting loud music nearly hit him, following that vehicle led him to discover a compound containing valuables. he stole the goods, visited a fence to sell them, and received another lead for an activity.

- Two hours passed without Hooker reaching the story mission he originally intended to test, that's how much fun there is to have in the GTA 6 open world, its insane!

- Hooker described this experience as one of the moments that convinced the team they had created something special.

- The game is designed to create these emergent gameplay experiences through overlapping NPC behaviors, police reactions, exploration, and criminal opportunities.

- Rockstar discovered it lacked the production capacity to create all the NPC content it wanted. To address this, Rockstar established a new Los Angeles studio dedicated to creating NPCs, employing writers, producers, and directors.

- Rockstar's leadership says the GTA 6 delays resulted from the immense complexity of bringing all the game's systems together, rather than one major technical problem.

- Some gameplay systems and design decisions were still being changed during the final months of development.

- Rockstar chose to delay the game rather than release a version that failed to meet its quality ambitions.

- Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick was reportedly shocked by the second delay but ultimately supported the decision.

- At Rockstar North, developers were heavily focused on bug fixing ahead of release, with internal progress indicators showing more resolved issues than outstanding ones.

- In September 2022, GTA VI suffered a massive leak after an attacker used phishing to access Rockstar's Slack communications.

- Dozens of unfinished gameplay videos were released publicly, exposing early development work.

- Rockstar developers described the leak as deeply invasive and emotionally difficult.

- The COVID-19 pandemic also significantly disrupted development, particularly performance capture.

- Several senior designers departed during development amid frustration over slow progress.

- Rockstar experienced another major leak in August 2026, despite introducing stricter security measures.
By 2024, Rockstar required employees to work five days a week in the office.

- Developers were prohibited from accessing company development servers and tools remotely, a policy Rockstar said was necessary for security.

- Rockstar intends to reconsider its remote-work policy after release, although a conventional hybrid arrangement is considered unlikely.

- Rockstar sought to eliminate the prolonged crunch periods associated with RDR2, which involved months of approximately 60-hour workweeks for some employees.

- The company introduced improved scheduling, additional hiring, and compensation or paid leave for extra hours.

- Leadership acknowledges that crunch was not entirely eliminated but claims working conditions improved considerably.

- Rockstar leadership says it will recognize a union if employees want one.

- Rockstar specifically rejected the rumor that development exceeded $1.5 billion.

- GTA VI's online component is expected to arrive in 2027, although Rockstar has not yet discussed it in detail.

So here's a big part: What is next for Rockstar?

- Rockstar believes GTA VI establishes a new technological and production foundation for its future games and content.

- The company says it has invested heavily in improving its engine, development tools, and production pipelines.

- Developers believe these improvements will allow them to create future content substantially faster.

- Rockstar's leadership says its next release should not require another eight years of development.

- The team points to GTA III and Vice City as an example of how a strong technological foundation can accelerate follow-up projects.

- Garbut says much of the fundamental technology has now been rebuilt and Rockstar does not intend to overhaul it again.

- The three development heads believe GTA VI represents the culmination of almost 30 years of accumulated experience.

Overall, this is a deeply interesting look inside of Rockstar and the development of GTA 6, it's clear that this game is now just the basis of what Rockstar intends to do going forward. I hope that with this foundation, they put out games like Bully 2, RDR3, GTA 7 and more much faster as they get back to faster releases.

Dear Secretary Bessent @SecScottBessent,

My name is Everett Stern. In 2010 I was a compliance officer at @HSBC. From a back office in New Castle, Delaware, I watched billions of dollars move to drug cartels, sanctioned regimes, and terrorist organizations. The enemies of the United States. I documented it, I escalated it, and when the bank would not act, I took it to the @FBI, the @CIA, and eventually the @SECGov.

The result was a $1.92 billion settlement. At the time, it was one of the largest in American history. It was also about five weeks of the bank’s profit. Not one banker was charged. Not one went to prison.

I paid a different price. I lost my career, my savings, and my place in the industry I had trained for. I was blacklisted. Every door in American finance closed at once. I slept on a camping cot in a 300 square foot apartment because I could not afford a bed, and I waited tables at @PFChangs to eat. I tell you this not for sympathy, but so you understand that I know exactly what it costs to do the right thing in American finance, and exactly how little the system does in return.

I made that sacrifice because I believed it would change something.

Yesterday, your department fined @BankofAmerica $1.2 billion for failing to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, some of it tied by your own findings to Chinese laundering networks, narcotics, and the southwest border, alongside 475 apparent sanctions violations touching Russia, Iran, and global terrorism. The bank admitted it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act.

Fourteen years after HSBC. A bank with “America” in its name. And once again, not one individual charged.

Secretary Bessent, I want to say plainly what I believe you already know. The fines are not working.

A fine is paid by shareholders, absorbed by the balance sheet, and forgotten by the next earnings call. Bank of America reported earnings this morning. Nobody who set the alert thresholds, nobody who decided the 2024 cease and desist could wait, nobody who chose the backlog over the law will lose a single thing they value. Their lives are untouched. That is the entire reason the behavior repeats.

This is money laundering. This is blood money. Money that reaches a cartel buys fentanyl that kills Americans. Money that reaches a terrorist organization buys the next attack. This country has fought a war on drugs and a war on terror for decades, at enormous cost in lives and treasure, and all the while we have allowed the financing to flow through institutions we charter and regulate. Cut off the money and we win. We have never seriously tried.

There is also a question of equal justice that I cannot let go.

Before I walked into the FBI building to report HSBC, I stopped in front of the Great Seal on the wall and read the words engraved beneath it: “Justice is the defense of our liberty.” I believed that. I still want to. But every day in this country, people go to prison for crimes that are nothing next to moving money for the people who want Americans dead. A suit, a title, and a corporate badge should not be a shield from the consequences that apply to everyone else. If a street dealer goes to prison for what he sells, the banker who moved the cartel’s money should be standing next to him.

I also want to raise something that is rarely said in these conversations. Why has no one inside Bank of America come forward the way I did? The answer is that everyone in American banking knows what happened to me, and to the whistleblowers who came after. The last person who spoke up is the only policy anyone believes. That is a culture problem, and it starts with leadership, in the banks and in the agencies that regulate them.

This is not a political issue. It has spanned administrations of both parties. It is a national security issue, and I am asking you to treat it as one.

Three things would change the math overnight.

Refer individuals for criminal prosecution. Not the analyst in the queue. The executives who set the thresholds and chose the risk. One banker in handcuffs would do more than every fine in Treasury’s history combined.

End “too big to jail.” An institution cannot be too big to fail and too big to jail at the same time. If it is the first, it must be held to a higher standard, not a lower one.

And if Bank of America will not act as America’s bank, review its charter. A national charter is a privilege granted on behalf of the American people. It should be conditioned on not moving money for the people trying to kill them.

Secretary Bessent, you said yesterday that these actions send a clear message that even the biggest institutions are not above the law. With respect, the institution was never the problem. The people inside it are above the law, and they know it. Until that changes, I will keep writing letters like this one, and the next bank will keep paying the next fine.

I gave up everything I had to stop this. I am asking you to use the power you have to finish it.

Respectfully,

Everett A. Stern 
HSBC Whistleblower

2109335218478108770.text:
A retired NASA engineer who had worked on the Space Shuttle program for 25 years was hired by SpaceX at age 62. He described the first week as the most disorienting experience of his professional life.

At NASA, a design change required 3 meetings, 2 committees, a review board, and 6 to 18 months of documentation. At SpaceX, his new supervisor said "if it works, build it. If it doesn't, change it by Friday."

He sat at his desk after the first day and called his wife. He told her he felt like a man who had been swimming with ankle weights for 25 years and someone just cut them off. He could move. He could decide. He could build something in the morning and test it in the afternoon. The constraint that he had accepted as the nature of aerospace engineering turned out to be the nature of bureaucracy.

Within 6 months he had contributed to more design iterations than he had completed in his last 5 years at NASA. Not because he was working harder. Because the time between having an idea and testing the idea collapsed from months to hours. The same brain. The same knowledge. A different operating system.

He described a specific moment where he proposed a modification to a Raptor engine component. At NASA, the proposal would have entered a queue. At SpaceX, the modification was machined by the end of the day and tested by the following morning. He watched his idea become a physical object in 18 hours. At NASA, 18 hours would not have been enough to schedule the first meeting to discuss whether to schedule a meeting.

He told an interviewer: "I didn't get smarter when I went to SpaceX. I got faster. The intelligence was always there. The system was in the way."

The difference between SpaceX and NASA is not talent. NASA has extraordinary talent. The difference is the time between a thought and a test. SpaceX compresses it. NASA elongates it. The same engineer produces 10x more at SpaceX than at NASA because the bottleneck was never the engineer. It was the meetings about the meetings about the work.

2110514044545171649.text:
A woman in Ohio called 911 because somebody was digging a grave in her backyard at 2 AM.

The dispatcher asked who was outside.

She said, “My husband.”

Dispatcher: “Ma'am, why is your husband digging a grave?”

Woman: “He says he's burying our dog.”

Dispatcher: “Did your dog pass away?”

Woman: “That's the thing. Our dog is sleeping right beside me.”

The dispatcher went quiet.

Dispatcher: “Are you sure that's your husband?”

Woman: “I've been married to him for 11 years. Of course I'm sure.”

Dispatcher: “Okay. Please stay inside. Officers are on their way.”

She hung up.

Then her 7-year-old son walked into the kitchen.

Son: “Mommy, why is Daddy digging again?”

Woman: “Again?”

Son: “He was digging yesterday too.”

Woman: “What?”

Son: “He told me not to tell you.”

She looked through the window.

Her husband was still digging.

There was a huge black bag beside the hole.

She opened the back door.

Woman: “Babe, what the hell are you doing?”

Husband: “Go back inside.”

Woman: “Why are you digging up our yard?”

Husband: “I'll explain tomorrow.”

Woman: “Is that a BODY in that bag?”

He stopped digging.

Husband: “Why would you even ask me that?”

Woman: “Because you're digging a damn grave at 2 AM!”

Husband: “Just go inside, please.”

She slammed the door.

Her son was standing behind her.

Son: “Mommy?”

Woman: “What, baby?”

Son: “Daddy said if you find out what's in the bag, we gotta move again.”

Her stomach dropped.

Woman: “What do you mean AGAIN?”

Son: “Like when we left our old house.”

They'd moved six months earlier.

Her husband said he'd gotten a better job.

She never questioned it.

Then the police arrived.

Officer: “Sir, step away from the shovel.”

Husband: “This is my property.”

Officer: “We received a call about suspicious activity.”

Husband: “From who?”

His wife stepped onto the porch.

Woman: “From me.”

He looked absolutely devastated.

Husband: “You called the COPS on me?”

Woman: “Open the bag.”

Husband: “Honey, please.”

Woman: “OPEN IT.”

The officer unzipped it.

Inside were women's clothes.

A purse.

A pair of heels.

And a framed wedding photo.

But the woman in the picture wasn't his wife.

Officer: “Sir, whose belongings are these?”

Husband: “My wife's.”

Woman: “EXCUSE ME?”

Husband: “My first wife.”

She almost laughed.

Woman: “You told me you were NEVER married before.”

Husband: “I know.”

Officer: “Where is your first wife now?”

He didn't answer.

Officer: “Sir?”

Husband: “She's dead.”

Woman: “WHAT?”

Husband: “She died twelve years ago.”

Officer: “Then why are you burying her belongings tonight?”

He started crying.

Husband: “Because she wasn't supposed to find them.”

Woman: “Find WHAT?”

He pointed toward the house.

Husband: “The letters.”

That's when her son came running outside holding a yellow envelope.

Son: “Mommy, is this what Daddy was looking for?”

Her husband turned completely pale.

The officer took the envelope.

Inside was a letter dated just three weeks earlier.

It read:

“I know what happened to your first wife. You have seven days to tell your new family, or I will.” .................

SpaceXAI’s Grok Voice 3.0 is the new leading Speech to Speech model, debuting at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 86.9, while also being competitive on latency

Grok Voice 3.0 is @spacexai 's successor to Grok Voice 2.0, a Speech to Speech model available through the SpaceXAI Realtime API at $0.08 per minute. We evaluated Grok Voice 3.0 with the Rex voice through the SpaceXAI Realtime API.

Key takeaways:

➤ Speech to Speech Index: Grok Voice 3.0 debuts at #1 at 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 82.6 and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 80.1. It is up on Grok Voice 2.0 at 81.3 (+5.6 points) and Grok Voice 1.0 at 73.7 (+13.2 points), released just under six months ago. The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference, and Task Success Rate

➤ Speech Agent Arena: Grok Voice 3.0 ranks #3 in preference at Elo 1070, behind Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Minimal (1100) and Gemini 3.8 Live (1088) and ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1057, and #1 on Task Success Rate at 94.8%, highest on the board, just ahead of Grok Voice 2.0 at 94.6%. Grok Voice 2.0 trails at Elo 1011

➤ Tau Voice: Grok Voice 3.0 takes the #2 spot on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 71.6%, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5% and ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 68.6% and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 59.3% - up from 56.5% for Grok Voice 2.0

➤ Big Bench Audio: Grok Voice 3.0 scores 98.5% on audio reasoning, ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 97.7% and Grok Voice 2.0 at 97.2%

➤ Speed: Average Time to First Audio on Big Bench Audio is 0.81 seconds for Grok Voice 3.0, well ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1.24s, GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 1.34s and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 1.35s, though slower than Grok Voice 2.0 at 0.70s

➤ Cost: Grok Voice 3.0 costs $4.80 per hour of input audio, the same as Grok Voice 2.0. That is above GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at $4.47 and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at $3.50, cheaper than GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at $5.83, and ~2.2x cheaper than GPT-Realtime-2.1 High at $10.75

Congrats to @elonmusk  and the @spacexai  team 🚀

Jensen reveals he first met the Founder of TSMC by cold calling their number off Yellow Pages

"I heard about this company in Taiwan, TSMC and UMC at the time. They were of course quite poor companies themselves, and they were barely making it." 

"TSMC was probably about $300 million, something like that. It's a tiny little company. I heard about Morris Chang. And so I tried to call their US office."

When @Starlink helped rescuers save nine fishermen from a flooding boat in Alaska.

The United States Coast Guard confirmed that all nine people aboard the Arctic Sea were rescued.

Their fishing boat had run aground near St. George Island in Alaska’s remote Bering Sea and was taking on water. Winds around 93 km/h and three-metre waves made it too dangerous for a nearby fishing boat, North Sea, to rescue the crew directly.

North Sea used Starlink to stay connected throughout the response. Its crew also provided updates to the Coast Guard. A Coast Guard helicopter lifted all nine fishermen to safety.

Starlink helped keep communications working during an emergency where nine lives were at risk.

This life-saving technology should be available in every part of the world.

2110398158844928332.text:
In July 1989, 3-month-old Ryan Stallings became so sick that his parents rushed him to a hospital in St. Louis.

Tests found antifreeze in his blood.

Doctors believed he had been poisoned, so Ryan was taken from his parents and placed in foster care. From then on, they could only see him during short, supervised visits.

In early September, just days after a visit in which his mother, Patricia, fed him a bottle, Ryan fell ill again. Police found antifreeze in the family's basement and arrested Patricia. On September 7, Ryan died.

At the time, Patricia was pregnant. In February 1990, while she was waiting for trial, she gave birth to a second son, David Jr. He was taken from her right away.

Soon, David Jr. developed the same symptoms, even though he had never been in his mother's care. This time, doctors found the real cause: a rare genetic disorder called methylmalonic acidemia, which can look like antifreeze poisoning on lab tests.

Even so, in January 1991, a jury convicted Patricia of first-degree murder, and she was sentenced to life in prison.

Months later, her story aired on "Unsolved Mysteries." A scientist watching the episode retested Ryan's blood and found no antifreeze at all. Ryan had suffered from the same disorder as his little brother.

In September 1991, prosecutors dropped the charges and apologized. Patricia had spent nearly two years behind bars for a crime that never happened.

I’m French. I want to talk to Americans who are about to vote Democrat. Not to insult you. To warn you.

I come from your future.

In France we did everything your progressive politicians promise. Free healthcare, free college, generous welfare, strong unions, heavy regulation, high taxes on the rich, a state that takes care of everything. Public spending close to 57% of GDP, one of the highest on the planet. On paper, it’s the dream.

Here’s what it looks like from the inside. France hasn’t passed a balanced budget since 1974. Our debt is above 3,300 billion euros. Interest on that debt is becoming one of the biggest items in the national budget. Our hospitals are collapsing despite record funding. Our schools rank lower every year. Young people with degrees can’t afford an apartment in the city they were born in. Our best engineers leave for London, Zurich and San Francisco. And the rich you wanted to tax? They left too, and took the jobs with them.

The promise was protection. The result is stagnation.

The worst part is that nobody in France voted for decline. Every single step sounded generous, compassionate, reasonable. One more program. One more regulation. One more tax to fund it. Each step alone makes sense. Fifty years of them, and you wake up in a country that can no longer build a nuclear plant on time or keep its streets safe.

I love America because it’s the one place on earth where people still believe they can build something from nothing. I came to Silicon Valley as a self-taught kid and it changed my life. That spirit is the most precious thing your country has.

Before you vote, ask yourself one question: is the program you’re voting for making America more like America, or more like France?

Trust me. You don’t want to be France.

2109922276569477181.text:
非洲真的很缺水吗？其实“懒”才是他们穷的根本原因。有数据显示，非洲地下水储量是地表的100倍，为何他们不挖井，而是到处找水？
我之前跟着一支海外工程队在那边待了快八个月，亲眼见过太多让人匪夷所思的事，说出来真的好多人都不敢信。我们当时的营地建在一片开阔的草地上，刚过去的时候要解决用水问题，队里找了个测水的师傅随便找了个地方打井，打到不到十二米就出了清水，水质甜得很，除了供我们队四十多个人吃喝洗澡，还能引出一垄水浇我们开出来的小菜园，天天浇水都用不完。
而离我们营地不到两公里的地方，就有一个百十来口人的部落村子，我第一次跟着采购去村里的时候，就看见全村人都围着一个半米深的泥坑接水，那水浑得放半小时都澄清不了，水面上还飘着虫子和牲畜的粪便，小孩渴了蹲下来直接舀了就喝，大人也不管，不少小孩隔三差五就拉肚子，缺药耽误着能拖出大病，看着真的让人心疼。我当时就问翻译，咱们这边打井出了这么多水，他们咋不来打一口？翻译笑笑说，你往后看就知道了，不是水的事。
没过多久工程闲下来，队长说反正咱们设备人都有，不如免费帮他们打一口井，也算做件好事，结果第一步就卡壳了。村长带着一群人堵在我们选好的井址，说这块地是他们部落的公用土地，要打井就得给他们十袋面粉五桶食用油外加两箱汽水，不然别想动土。我们队里想着反正也不多，给就给了，就当换一口井给村里人用，这点东西对我们来说不算什么。
接下来要找几个当地人帮忙打下手搬东西，我们说好一天给一斤玉米面两瓶汽水，这个待遇在当地已经够一个三口之家吃饱喝足了，比他们自己瞎晃赚得多太多，结果来了五个人，干了不到四十分钟，全都撂挑子坐到树底下乘凉去了，说太阳太晒，会晒伤皮肤，祖宗规矩就是正午不能干活，要等太阳落山再干活。我们想着入乡随俗那就等，结果太阳落山之后，连个人影都没见着，第二天上午好不容易来了三个，还要求必须先给汽水玉米面，不给就不动手，我们给了之后，三个人晃悠着挖了不到半米，又坐下来歇着聊天了，一聊就是一上午，第三天干脆全都不来了，托人带话来说拿到的吃的够喝够吃好几天，先回家休息，吃完了再来。
最后没办法，我们工程队自己上手，不到十天就打出了一口出水稳定的井，还给他们在井口安了简易的提水架，放了两个大木桶，跟村长说以后大家随便来打水，只要别往井里扔垃圾就行。一开始村里人可开心了，天天排着队来打水，结果半个月不到，井口就堵了，我们过去一看，大大小小的树枝石头烂叶子堵了小半井，原来大家打完水垃圾随手就扔在井口边上，下雨一冲全进去了。我们免费帮他们清干净，反复跟村长和村民说不要扔垃圾，要保持井口干净，结果不到两个月，又堵了，之后村长干脆来找我们，说井坏了，你们再帮我们打一口新的吧，那语气说得理所当然，好像我们就该天天给他们收拾烂摊子。
我之前还碰到过一次，营地的围墙坏了一段，找了四个当地工人来修，说好一天干完给对应的工钱，结果四个工人八点开工，九点就歇着喝茶，十点吃早饭，十二点要睡午觉，睡到下午三点才起来，干了不到一小时又说要回家喂孩子，一天下来只码了不到五块砖，第二天还过来要全额工钱，说我们没给他们提供茶和饼，所以干得慢，钱不能少给，当时给我们队长气得直接把他们赶走了。
待得久了我才发现，这种事真的不是个例。有个二十多岁的小伙子天天来我们营地卖野果，我们看他挺活络，就说你干脆天天给我们营地送菜，我们一个月给你固定的工钱，比你卖野果稳定多了，结果他干了三天，第四天就不见了，过了一周晃悠过来，问他为啥不来，他说前三天赚的钱够花了，在家歇着花完了再来。还有国际援助组织免费给他们发蔬菜种子，教他们开荒种地，说种好了够全村吃大半年，结果一半种子被他们煮着吃了，剩下的随便往地里一撒，既不浇水也不除草，长不出来就接着等着发援助。
真的，很多人说非洲穷是因为气候不好历史遗留问题，可我们明明看到脚底下十几米就是清水，储量够整个村子用几十年，有人免费帮你打出来，就只要随手维护一下都做不到。他们不是没有力气，跑出去找野果跳篝火舞能折腾一整天，一说到干活赚饭吃，半小时就喊累；也不是没有资源，地下水摆在那，援助摆在那，就是不肯伸手去动。
我待了八个月见过好多口废弃的援助井，全都是打完没两年没人维护废了，当地人宁愿背着水桶走三四公里去接脏雨水，也不肯花半天时间清一清堵了的井口。你说这到底是延续了几千年的靠天吃饭的生活方式已经刻进骨子里改不了，还是真的就是“懒”才导致一直摆脱不了穷呢？你怎么看这件事？
